utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And good morning to everyone both in and just outside of the courtroom. Is the Defence ready to continue the examination of the witness Moroz? Mr. Usher, could you then please escort the witness into the courtroom. I inform the parties that where the witness has expressed his preference to testify in English, that there is one interpreter who will not translate everything but is standby in the booth whenever there will be any problem and that there is a second interpreter standby, but a bit more distance whenever we would decide that we need full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Moroz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your examination will now continue, and I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Pilipovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Moroz. Yesterday towards the end of our working hours we had your answer about how you as the chief of the mission which went out to make repairs, you told us about how you organised your work, and I believe you said that as the chief of that section, you communicated with local authorities, both civilian and military. Did I understand your answer well?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- it's not quite so, because I was not chief of the section. I was mission commander. So because in our section there were five mission commanders. We each fulfilled orders of chief of section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to say that I did not say "sector," because I know that you were with an engineering section and that your missions -- but I do not know. I suppose it must be a mistake in the interpretation, since you are following the transcript. But let us not waste time. You communicated with local, civilian, and military commanders. Tell us, on what basis did you communicate with civilian and military commanders?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I would like to say that my contacts with military local commanders was very limited, and I got permission to proceed with any engineer mission only through liaison officers who contacted both warring sides, and only after both sides gave their green light for engineer mission, I got permission from my boss to go to any -- any of these point where a mission should be done. And as far as for civilian parties concerned, I connected with them more closely because in the morning before going to the mission, I went to the company which was authorised to provide any repair job. It was a sewage company, water supply Sarajevo company, electricity company, and so on. I contacted chief of the companies, agreed any of matters which should be done to renovate any of the objects, took civilian officers of the company, and then I went to the place of the repair and did the job over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Moroz, your answer tells me that by and large you cooperated principally with the civilian authorities when it came to your missions.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that after you would be given your assignment from the representatives of companies, you told us you went out into the field. Can you tell us how did you hire workers, and did you hire workers from both sides? When I say "both sides," I mean the Serb and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I wouldn't say "hire," because usually it was the willingness of civilian authorities to provide -- to do renovation just to ensure normal life for civilian people. That is why it was their initiative mostly -- it was their initiative to ask UNPROFOR to organise such a mission. That is why usually a chief of such companies knew what should be done, would work a team to give us for the mission, and what repair parts should be used during the mission. And before the mission, they often ask UNPROFOR to provide the repair parts which they do not have at the moment, which they didn't have at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, can you tell us whether when going out for repair work, whether did you form some mixed working teams. Was there any need for that?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. When mixed teams were formated -- and usually it was done for two reasons. Sometimes one of the warring sides provided repair parts, and they want -- they wanted to be sure that these repair parts are really installed in the object. It was one of the reasons. The other was that the greater part of jobs were done just on the front line. And during the periods where fire exchange was very intensive, workers and their chiefs were afraid that a provocation could be -- could take place. And just to avoid that, it was widely announced that a mixed team will work on the spot. And local commanders informed about that all soldiers just to avoid any sporadic -- sporadic fire. So the second reason is for the sake of safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just told us that you performed the repairs, if I understand you well, on the front line, where exchanges of fire were frequent. Can you tell us how frequently did you go out to do these repairs during your tour of duty? Can you tell us that? When I say "frequently," I mean did you go out once a week, every day?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I went for the mission nearly each day. And as far as I understood your question, you asked if this mission were disrupted due to the exchange of fire, how often they were disrupted. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that these missions were often cancelled because of fire exchange, but usually it was once in two weeks, something like that. But of course during the year of my staying in Sarajevo, there were more tense periods when mission cancellations [Realtime transcript read in error "consolidations"] were more frequent and a quiet period. For instance, summer 1994, when -- I don't remember when any mission was cancelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, I heard the witness say "mission cancellations," rather than "consolidations." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cancellation. Cancellation. So that is the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I gathered what you said right, once you started working at a particular place, you would have to stop working because of exchanges of fire.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You got right, because the priority was the safety of workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, as you say, fire was exchanged, could you personally determine where the fire came from and who started that fire, say?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a couple of times mission cancellation was due to the mortar fire exchange, and we had ingoing and outgoing shells. But we were just between the fires, between the fire because we were on the front line and the targets on both sides were a little bit deeper in both territories. And several times we were shot at definitely by gunfire, but frankly speaking, I had such feeling that UNPROFOR mission wasn't a target. It was just for the sake to cancel the mission, because all traces of bullets were close to the team, to UNPROFOR soldiers, just -- so those people who shoot, they only wanted to scare it and cancel the mission. As far as the second part about who fired, it's very difficult to say because the direction of the fire always was from the area either neutral zone, so-called, or from the direction where both warring sides can shoot. That is why I cannot tell you for sure either it were Serbian soldiers or Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us - and you understand what sides we're talking about - so on which side did you perform most repairs of electric supply lines? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or areas where you went more often.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can, because you see, companies -- different companies were located on different territories. For instance, sewage company was purely Muslim because it was inside the city, and electrical company was purely -- consisted from purely Serbian workers because it was located on the Serbian territory. But the -- it doesn't mean that -- for instance, sometimes Muslim workers worked on their Serbian territory and vice versa. But the greater repair job in electricity lines were done on Serbian territory because pylons renovation -- I don't know why, but pylons were mostly damaged on Serbian territory in different places and wire cut off was very often -- so wire renovation was very often done in, it seems to me, Vogosca, so near the Volkswagen plant. Near the Volkswagen plant there was a substation, and near the substation very often wires were cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you tell us that the chief damage to pylons occurred on the Serb side, were you able to establish what was the cause of the damage of the pylons and whether it resulted in power cuts in some parts of the city?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason of the pylon renovation was mortar shell explosion just near -- near the pylon. And that is why workers dismantled the damaged one and then they gathered it, so renovated. And in fact, they did a new one. It was a rather difficult job. And usually it took one week or more. So of course the damage of these pylons caused electricity power cut off the main city because all electricity lines to the city were -- so all the lines came from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your previous answer you told us also that you performed most of the repairs in Vogosca, where also most damages occurred, where supply lines were cut off. Did you know what was the effect of the damage of those electric lines in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the main effect was that a great part of the city was out of electricity for the time of the repair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know what caused the damage of these cables in Vogosca which then had such an effect as you indicated, that is, power cuts?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So sometimes it was gunfire, and so the damage was not very big. Just one of the wires was cut. And the other reason was mortar fire from the Muslim side in the direction of Volkswagen plant, because as far as I know -- so I'm sure of that because Muslim workers often told me that there were rumours inside the city that on that plant an ammunition workshop was organised. I've been to that plant during the mission, and I hadn't seen any working activity on the plant, because it was seriously damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moroz, in the course of your missions, did you also provide security around some reservoirs -- or rather, was there water supply cut off and did you do something with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. So I had a number of missions in the area -- it seems to be Ilidza. So there were -- not far from the river there were special wells, special fields where pumping motors pushed water to the reservoir which was on the highest hill of Sarajevo, and from that reservoir, as far as I remember, it was an area called Mojmilo -- from that reservoir water came to the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, during your stay there, did you receive any information concerning any possible problems in some parts of the city in terms of supplying water to the civilian population? And if so, do you know how and where was the civilian population able to obtain water in a situation where the reservoirs were not operational and neither were water pumps?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the system of water supply was organised the following way: Water pumps were pumping water from the area of Ilidza to Mojmilo, and then officers of my section followed the situation in that reservoir. Each morning and each evening one of the officers went to the reservoir and closed or opened special wells just to provide the city with water. So in the evening we closed the reservoir just to make some stock -- water stock in that reservoir during the night, and in the morning we opened it. When pumping motors, engines were not operational just because of lack of-- sometimes because of lack of repair parts, sometimes because of the electricity -- there was not electricity to work, so there was no pumping water and there was a lack of water in the city. But I cannot say that the civilians had no water at all because the reservoir was very high and pipes -- water pipelines were rather long. There was water inside tubes, and in the low part of the city on the first -- on the ground floor very nearly -- it was always some water in the city. The only difficulties for civilians was that they had to take water in reservoir and then go upstairs to their apartments, so of course it was difficult for many of them. But nevertheless, to drink water -- drinking water was always available inside the city. Moreover, in the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, I would like us to be a bit more brief in view of the time available to us. But I will put this question to you: Did you know that in certain parts of the city there were certain sites where civilians waited to get water when the water supply was cut off, either because there was no electricity and the pumps didn't operate? Did you know that there was a site in town where civilians gathered to get water? Did you know of these sites?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the moment, I cannot specify those sites, but I saw myself that there were places inside the city where water was more frequently available. So usually it was very low places of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your recollection, can you tell us what were those sites? Do you remember them?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I saw -- one of the sites was not far from PTT. I cannot remember, unfortunately, this -- the name of the street. And a couple of sites were in the old city, not far from the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say a "a couple of other sites in the old city," could you tell us, if you remember, what were those sites? Where were they located in the old city? Do you remember a site where citizens could go and get water?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember -- I can show you in the city, but now I don't remember the street names of that site. Moreover, I know that there was a big reservoir, water reservoir on the beer plant. I know that for sure because I visited beer plant just to make an agreement for Ukrainian Battalion getting water from that reservoir. So there were great water shortage in Ukrainian Battalion in Tito barracks, and it was an agreement with a special truck, water truck, each day water was provided from beer plant. But I do not know if civilians can take water from beer plant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, you just told us about the beer plant, the brewery --

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brewery, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Which is the place where you obtained water. During your stay there, did you happen to hear that that area and the brewery had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, when I've been to brewery I could not remember that great damage was caused by that plant. I don't remember that. And I did not hear that brewery was shelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you had information, whether you heard that in the vicinity of the brewery -- or within the brewery itself there was a workshop that manufactured ammunition? And if you happened to hear this, who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic. I again have to stress that once a leading question is put to a witness, repair is hardly possible. So therefore, would you really refrain from it, because the Chamber might say that the witness cannot answer the question and then perhaps valuable information would not be available to the Chamber due to procedural problem that should not have risen. I'll ask the question to the witness. About activities in the brewery, do you know anything about it? I think you said that -- do you know anything about activities within the brewery? Was there any activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say -- I have been there for two times, and I haven't seen any activity on the brewery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next question: Did you hear from anyone else that there had been any activity, brewing beer or whatever activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So Muslim workers from -- so from water supply company told me that in the old city - I can't [Realtime transcript read in error "can"] specify the place - were workshops for -- ammunition workshops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not specifically the brewery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not brewery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, in view of your previous answers to the questions put by me, I took it that you had contacts both with the Muslim and the Serb side in your work. Can you tell us, what was that cooperation like with both sides?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cooperation was -- I think that very productive because the greater part of the missions I participated in were successful, and we managed to renovate various objects, either electricity lines or water supply systems or -- or others. And so as far as for workers concerned, all of them worked normally, and usually they did their best to renovate the object. So I should say that it was normally because both parts suffered without these civilian objects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the sake of the transcript, page 11, line 20, it reads: "I can specify the place," where I heard the witness say "I cannot specify the place," which is also logic in the context. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So only -- as far as I remember, there was only one period -- it was winter 1994, January/February, was when the situation on the front line was very tense and fire exchange was very frequent. Several times Muslim workers under the different pretexts avoided going to the front line, and they very often warned me not to visit this or that city area just because of the attack preparation from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about the cooperation with the warring sides, can you tell us whether you remember some individuals with whom you had contact most frequently in that period of time while you were doing repairs.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will try to remember the names, but I would like to warn you that a lot of time has passed and I can misspell -- mispronounce some of the names. So I remember Velimir Radunovic or something like that. It was workers' chief on electricity plant. So he was chief of team of Serbian workers which were engaged in pylon renovation -- electricity pylon renovation. Then very often I contacted vice-president of the railway company. We were engaged in tram line renovation inside the city. His name was Muhamed, but I do not remember his family name. Who else? Several times I visited gas company on Serbian side. The name of the person I spoke with was -- it seems to me Krajisnik. At least, I very well remember that he knew Russian perfectly. He studied in the Soviet Union. So I do -- I do remember these guys, but I do not remember the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moroz, you have told us that you were in charge of tram lines and the gas company. I would like to ask you this: In that period of time, in 1993 and up until October of 1994, do you know whether trams operated during that period of time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after my arrival in Sarajevo in October 1994, tram line renovation was the greatest project of all engineer section by that period. We started the job in December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. You said after your arrival in October 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1993. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we started tram line renovation, and it ended -- it was done in spring 1994. I do not remember exactly the month, but it was rather warm already when the first tram was -- went through the line. Well, during the winter, periodically the tram line renovation was stopped due to various reasons. But nevertheless, it was a long-lasting project.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Sarajevo, meaning up until October of 1994, did you personally have information to the effect that trams were shot at and that result of that, trams were damaged? Did you personally have such information? And if so, who did you receive it from?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a special agreement from both warring sides not to -- not to shoot at trams, and during a couple of weeks when the first tramway was put into order, each tram wagon was accompanied by APC. So it was moving just parallel to -- just along the tram line, just to shield the wagon. But as far as I remember, no shooting took place during those several -- couple weeks, and then it was taken a decision to stop escorting trams, and I do not remember any cases when anybody was killed or wounded, among passengers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moroz, you have also told us that you had contacts with the representatives of the gas company. Was that related to the gas supply to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way? What information did you have concerning the gas supply to the city, and where was the city supplied with gas from?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I got an order from my chief to visit first gas company inside the city, and I had conversation with the chief - I do not remember his name - to clarify the reasons there were not gas in the city. So the answer was that first Russia cut -- or diminished, reduced gas supply to Bosnia; and the second, that gas pipelines in some places were damaged. And due to that, gas pressure is very low in the city. After that I went to the Serbian side and spoke to -- I mentioned this man Krajisnik. And he confirmed that information, that gas supply is reduced to a great extent. And there were damages on the line, but due to low pressure, it's very difficult to find the places of the leak, gas leak on the lines. So only two times I've been involved in such missions and -- so no other missions I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, during your tour of duty, did you have occasion when you went out to do repairs to establish that as a result of a power outage or water supply cut off was -- ensued as a result of a deliberate action?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally me, no. Usually it was the section chief who examined personally pipelines, and very often he was -- he came from that mission very in a bad mood because on Muslim side wells were cut off and -- so in -- there was water in Mojmilo reservoir, but somewhere in the middle on the way to the city wells were cut -- were closed, and that is why civilians couldn't take water. For all of us it was very strange and unexplainable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just answered my questions concerning the water supply. Now, did you have any information as to in which sites certain reservoirs were closed, reservoirs used to supply water to the population? Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that information I had from my boss. It was just somewhere in the middle from Mojmilo to the -- from Mojmilo Hill to the old city, somewhere there, but I don't know where exactly. There were a number of wells, so -- dozens of wells. So in -- each time -- he told that each time he went to check them, another well was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, during your stay there, did you personally receive any protests concerning the lack of power due to the fact that either side deliberately had cut it off? Did you ever receive such protests? And if so, what were you able to establish pursuant to such protests?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So usually, as far as I remember, it was their -- our G2 section was receiving all such kinds of protests. And after that they informed my chief about such protests. But very often after the receiving of such protests, we started contacting both sides to find the reason of the electricity cutoff. And as far as I remember, nearly always the reason was just damage on the line. And usually the next day or -- I went to the pylons or somewhere else just to renovate it. I cannot say that it was a deliberate cutoff somewhere on the substation or something like that, because each time we found the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moroz. I understood that during your tour of duty in that one year while you were there, you were in some parts of town -- or you went to some parts of town, and I believe that you said that you went to a part of town where the brewery was and that you took part in repairing damaged tram lines. Am I to understand that you visited both sides of the city -- on both sides of the city?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've asked you whether you went to the part of town under the control of the BH army, that is, under Muslim control. Did you go to that part of town and did you walk around when you were not on duty, that is, when you were not carrying out your duties? And what was your view of the situation there? First of all, did you see armed men in that part of the city?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So during the first half of my tour of duty, it was prohibited for UN personnel to move around the city being out of duty. But each morning I went out to the mission, and I moved around the city and outside the city a lot. That is why I saw the situation in the city, so saw people in the street, and I saw BH soldiers in the old city, as well as on Serbian side, so Serbian soldiers I saw during the mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, the soldiers that you saw on the Bosnian side, as you say, and you saw them in the city, were they bearing arms and were you able to observe whether they were wearing uniforms and what kind of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I saw Muslim soldiers. They -- during the missions, because a lot of missions were just inside the old city in the narrow streets. Very often soldiers came to us, so just to speak something about -- they were very proud about their arms. They showed their guns, automatic guns, so -- and I should say that the situation during my tour of duty changed. When I just arrived, so their uniform was very -- and ammunition was very mixed. Sometimes it was very old; sometimes it was semi-civilian -- I mean, about uniforms, semi-civilian, semi-military. But when I was leaving, so soldiers were dressed in very good uniform, something -- it was, I think, produced somewhere in Europe, European type, camouflage. And their small arms also became -- so they already had new small arms. It seems to me they were German light gunfires -- automatic guns. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, when you answered the question in relation to the soldiers and when you described them in that part of the city, during that period of time during your stay, did you also see civilians in the town? And if you did, on what locations did you see them? Did you speak to them? Did you have an opportunity to speak to them?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I saw a lot of civilians, and I saw them all around the city. The only thing I should say, that in dangerous places there were less civilians. The most dangerous place in the city was the main street. We called it --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I don't have the interpretation. So I don't know what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what the problem is with the interpretation. Is the -- can you now hear me in a language you understand, Ms. Pilipovic, or still not?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were about to -- I don't know where it stopped, but the witness -- I'll just read the transcript for you, Ms. Pilipovic. The witness said, "Well, of course I saw a lot of civilians, and I saw them all around the city. The only thing I should say, that in dangerous places there were less civilians. The most dangerous place in the city was the main street. We called it --" and there the transcript stopped. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sniper Strasse, we called it. I know the street very well because the greater part of tram line was on that street, and I took a lot of missions on the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you told me that you saw civilians, were you able to observe how the civilians were dressed?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say it was something unusual. They were usually dressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, you now told us in your answer that the street where you went often, where civilian movement was restricted because of sniper activity. Can you tell us, what do you know about sniper activity in that part of the city or, rather, in that street where you went?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only sniper activity. It was also mortar -- mortar shelling. Well, there were a lot of rumours about sniper activity, and several times our missions also were shot at. But I think it were not snipers because we were very open, and if any sniper wanted to kill anybody from our mission, it would be done for sure. Well, after the mission very often I was asked by commanders what side our mission was shot at. I should say that it was very hard to determine it because in the city -- so sound from the shot comes from -- from alternatively -- from different directions. And usually we were shot at from the neutral zone or in the area which just was the front line. That is why I cannot say for sure what side we were shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, you also spoke about firing on members of the UN. You yourself, did you know anything about an event or an incident when fire was opened on UN members?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sure. It was a rather frequent case. And our missions I told you also were shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the previous answer, you told us that this was not the case just in that street, that it wasn't -- the movement wasn't just restricted because of firing, but you also said that there was mortar shelling there. Do you remember what you said?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally during your stay, did you know about firing from mortars? And if you did, could you tell us in which situations.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during my missions, we were not fired -- our missions were -- as far as I remember, were not fired by mortars. Usually it was just exchange -- fire exchanged between warring sides. And we were -- at that moment we were somewhere in the middle. But the greater mortar activity was during the night, and very often just close to PTT building where I was staying during the night, Muslim side -- Muslim soldiers fired from mortar and then it was an answer from Serbian side. Nearly -- especially during winter 1994, nearly each other day the night started from the mortar exchange. And the same story was with Tito barracks, where Ukrainian Battalion was located. Officers complained to me that it's hard to sleep because very often fire exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You now told us about two locations that you know about where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. The transcript is not quite clear, and I'd like to ask the witness to repeat that part of his answer so that there's no confusion. You told us -- and I'm reading -- "and very often just close to the PTT building where I was staying during the night, Muslim soldiers fired from --" and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it reads on the transcript, "mortar." Whereas I understand you to say "motor." And I do understand vehicles or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, from hand mortar. Mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mortar. Yes. That's good. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Moroz, you told us that you were in a position, you were in a situation that you knew that there was firing from mortars by the Muslim side on the PTT building where you were and that that was at night. Did you know -- did you have an opportunity to know -- were you able to know what type of mortars these were and how frequently did this occur? You set the dates as being in January/February, in winter I think you said in 1994. During this period, how frequently did this occur that you know of?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know because I lived there, and so it was rather a loud explosion, outgoing mortar fire, and that is why it's -- we could hear it, everybody, very clearly because usually it was done at night. I haven't seen it myself, but due to the sound, it was not a very big mortar. Usually a couple of shots, and then silence. And in five, ten minutes Serbs -- the Serbian side fired back. It was very often story, especially during the winter. Near -- sometimes every night; sometimes every other night. So something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, for the transcript, Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask, perhaps assisted by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I ask your attention for page 21, line 18, where part of your question was that the answer of the witness would have been that there was fire from mortars by the Muslim side on the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, from. From.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From, yes. So that -- I don't know what your question in the original language was, but as is was written here it does not reflect the testimony of the witness. But I do understand that it's clarified now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should probably specify. From the vicinity of PTT building, because it was some close territory which nobody was admitted in, but just near the line, this fence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. Perhaps may I ask you: We are approximately ten minutes from the break. As far as my account goes, there would be another 20 minutes approximately left. Would that be the time you'd need or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Moroz, you also spoke about knowing that Muslims fired from mortars at night on members of the Ukrainian Battalion. Can you tell us, what kind of information did you have? Where was fire coming from, mortar fire at night?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- if I may, I wonder whether it's a problem with the interpretation, but it goes "mortars at night on members of the Ukrainian Battalion," but that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, if there's any doubt as to the source, could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a mistake again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please reformulate your question -- or if it is a mistake in translation, would you then please repeat your question so that we --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, you told us that you had information about mortar activity by the Muslim side, that you received that information from representatives of the Ukrainian Battalion. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you receive that from and what kind of information did you receive regarding these kind of incidents?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the greater part of military escorts I went on mission with were from Ukrainian Battalion, and officers which went with me, so we had conversations, we discussed the life inside Sarajevo, and they complained about that regular activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have information while speaking to them or did you receive such information where did BH army members fire from?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, just near the fence or near the buildings of Tito barracks, just close to that, probably 50 metres, 20 metres. I cannot say. But something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, can you tell us, during your stay during your tour of duty in Sarajevo, did you have any knowledge whether during this period there were some incidents during which according to the information - if you've had them - civilians had died? Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that from time to time civilians died during fire exchange, and once I was -- so I helped a man who was shot at near our place of mission and with APC we delivered him to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or did you have that information whether, during the period while you were there, there was an incident that occurred on which occasion civilians were killed as a result of shelling? Did you have such information?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard several times that civilians, sometimes children, were killed during exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally, do you remember an incident while you were in Sarajevo and do you have information that during such an incident many civilians were killed during your stay between October 1993 and October 1994?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the greater incident was explosion at the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, you personally, what information did you have about that explosion that happened on Markale market? And if you do have any information, where did you -- who did you get it from and what information was that?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it will be a little bit long answer. First I have had -- I've seen the results of the explosion on TV, so nearly 20 or 30 minutes after the explosion all that was live report on local TV. Well, the next day I had mission not far from the marketplace, and I visited that and just saw -- examined the place of the explosion. And for me -- so on TV it was told that it was a mortar shell. After I've seen what I saw, the marketplace, for me it was very strange that it was -- the cause of the explosion was identified as mortar shell because it was inside the city and buildings are rather high, and so to my mind trajectory of the shell -- so that the place of the explosion couldn't be at the place it was. After, it were a number of inspection teams organised, UN inspection teams. And nearly one month later I had a conversation with UNMO, a Russian officer. It seems to me his name was Alexei Rumeltsov, it seems to me, but probably I am wrong -- who participated in the expert inspection from UNMO side. And he told me it was definitely proved that it could not be a mortar explosion shelled from Serbian side. The reasons were -- it were different reasons, but all of them excluded the possibility of mortar shell explosion shot from Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would you still need -- how much time would you still need, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will consult my colleague. Perhaps another couple of questions. Perhaps 10, 15 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes would be approximately the time you indicated. May I then take it that you'll conclude in ten minutes. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When the witness is brought in, I remind the Defence that they would still give an indication as to the time when the detailed survey of subjects could be delivered. Ms. Pilipovic, I asked you yesterday to tell me this as the first thing in the morning. We're already halfway the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence is ready. And I've agreed with my colleague who will only tell us when it would be convenient for the Defence to present its position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there an agreement between the parties on the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not that I know, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber has invited the Defence to indicate when it thought that it could provide the information required, and then we'll perhaps at a later stage hear from the Prosecution what their view is on that. But perhaps we could first know time -- date and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if we are talking about soon or very soon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was mentioned yesterday. The Defence wishes to say we discussed it yesterday with Mrs. Pilipovic. We have taken note of the decision. We were told that this was the decision of the Chamber, and we'd like to thank you. The Defence's position between tonight and tomorrow, we shall submit a submission under Article 63, and I believe that our submission concerning your decision will reach you either tonight or tomorrow, and that is the reason because -- that is the reason why we have not yet made up our minds regarding this matter. The Defence continues, Mr. President, to take good note of the decision, but we believe it is an absolute right of all the accused before this Chamber to remain silent until the end and that includes until the hearing of the expert witnesses, and we therefore wish to appeal against your decision. We believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I did not ask you whether the Defence wants to appeal against the decision. We'll wait and see whether that happens. But you now spent 15 lines where I just asked you when you would be able to provide the information of which you now tell me that you do not want to provide that information. Okay. Fine if you appeal against the decision. I'm just asking you a very simple question; that is, you were invited yesterday to tell the Chamber when you would provide the information that the Chamber instructed the Defence to provide. And if you say, "I'm not going to tell you," that's a clear answer. Then the Chamber will have to decide what to do. But this is, as I perhaps told you before -- is not a debating club, but this is a court where a decision has been given yesterday. And of course you can ask for a certificate for appeal. And if you do not agree, you can do whatever you want, but this is not a moment for debate. I'm just asking you what would be the time where, as I indicated, I invited the Defence to give its opinion on that before the Chamber will decide on when the Defence has to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I will answer very clearly. I thought to have understood that we could not and we -- it is not that we do not want to, we could not do it. And if you ask us why, I can explain that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you're not giving the indication when you will provide the Prosecution with the information the Chamber has decided you would have to give to the Prosecution. Your reference to Article 63, by the way, is relatively unclear to me, because that's about questioning an accused before --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I must have mentioned 72 and 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my co-counsel will use these last ten minutes that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. I'd like to go back to what you said a while ago, that is, on page 6, line 4 when you said that very often the shelling happened and that it very frequently hit the area where the presidency was inside the city itself. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not remember speaking about presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But it is the -- it is how we at times call the Muslim forces. You did not mention them. But do you remember that you said that these shellings were frequent from the -- originating from the forces called the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I spoke that there were cases that Muslim forces did -- mortar shelled from the vicinities of PTT. It means headquarters -- UNPROFOR headquarters Sarajevo, and Tito barracks where Ukrainian Battalion was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What I wanted you to tell us is the following: Were you able to establish -- to determine the calibres from which those shots were fired? Was it just one calibre weapon, different calibres, and which ones?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should say judging from the sound, it was not a big calibre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate a specific calibre, in terms of millimetres?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to be more precise with regard to an answer that you have already given concerning the shots which came from the neighbourhood of the PTT. First, do you know whether around the PTT building there was a perimeter? And in that case, what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a fence around the PTT building, and it was guarded. Nobody from outside except UN personnel allowed to go inside that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then I will ask you this: You said that you heard shots near this building, near the PTT building. Was it a regular event or not or what?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was regular during a definite period. It was summer and early spring 1994. Later I do not remember that it was very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Witness, my question was as follows. It didn't have to do with time. It had to do with the normal character -- that is -- or not, that is acceptable or non-acceptable fire. Fire which came from places near the PTT building, was it regular or irregular? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I would say that it was regular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say regular or irregular?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In French I understood that you said "regular." Would it be acceptable from the point of -- but it was not frequent. Regular in terms of regulations of the right. That is, in other words, did the Muslim forces have the right to fire from places in the neighbourhood of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this is a, I would say -- rather a legal issue. And would you please first establish what would be the specific basis of knowledge for this witness to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you -- were you told about the possibilities, not only technical but also administrative and legal possibilities, that the parties had to open fire from certain areas close to certain types of buildings, such as, for instance, hospitals, official UN buildings, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I do not know about any agreements about specific areas which should be not shot at. The only exception of that was airport area, which were a number of meetings, so just avoid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I think that this is not exactly the information that you're seeking, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Do you have any personal opinion as to whether militarily it is acceptable to fire from a place which is -- was a short distance from the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my opinion is the following: From the military point of view, there was no use firing mortar shelling from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would there be -- I think that was the question. Would there be any -- apart from whether it had any use or not, would there be any prohibition to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to be no. So they have the right to shoot from that area. So nobody forbid it. There was not any agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was not any agreement with UNPROFOR with Muslims not to shoot from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But would you say that on the basis of the laws of war there would be a prohibition to do so even without an agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Always just in war and love.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear that answer. So -- but did you have any opinion as to -- apart from any agreement, whether it would be permissible to fire from a place close to the PTT building by one of the warring factions, in the case the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I only can judge about the goal of such firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on the legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, I will change the subject. Witness, you told us that you frequently went into town and that you were able to see civilians saying that they were dressed normally. But because Sarajevo was not like any other place, my question is: When at that time you saw civilians, did they -- did they wear pieces of clothing which were disparate? Did they have types of clothing? Did you notice anything particular?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was nothing unusual which I can mention now. So they were dressed normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like now with regard to the civilian life in Sarajevo, I'd like to hear your comments about how people lived at that time in Sarajevo. That, did they patronise -- did they go to restaurants? Did they eat out? Did they visit public places, and so on and so forth? What can you tell us about the public life, about the street life?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got your question. So to my great surprise, during the cease-fire periods, public life emerged nearly the next day. And so in a couple of days during the cease-fire period dozens of cafe were opened, so peoples started working inside the city, so -- and life went on rather intensefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that you were able to see - I mean the civilians - did you have the impression that they were -- that their behaviour could not be compared to the behaviour of such population elsewhere in Europe?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I had such feeling that during the cease-fire people did their best to forget about the war situation they were in. That is why they tried to behave normally, dress normally, like they did before war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answers my question to you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last question: Did you happen to see weapons in the city of, of whatever nature? And if yes, what did you see and where?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually I had close contacts with civilians inside the old city, because streets were narrow and it was a safe area to walk. As for the weapons, I already told you that in the first period of my tour of duty I saw that weapons was rather obsolete -- I mean on Muslim side inside the city. Sometimes it were shotguns of Second World War period. But at the time just before I left Sarajevo, I could say that at that period soldiers were dressed in new uniforms and they had new small fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But Mr. President, before I start, I would like to place on record the fact that this witness testified about the Markale market explosion, and contrary to the guidance given by the Bench, the Defence has not mentioned the fact that the witness would be testifying about this incident in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as my recollection goes, there was no specific question about Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it came up during the -- one of the answers of the witness rather than that any specific question has been put to him in this respect. So that's on record then as well. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you spoke with a Russian UNMO who provided you some information about an investigation conducted into the shelling of the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please give the full name of that Russian officer, and could you please spell that name out.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you that as far as I remember, because many years have passed, and I can misspell the name, but it seems to me his name was Alexei Rumeltsov. So he stayed in that area like UNMO for a couple of months, and I think that in the records we should clarify the name, because I told you that he was -- as he told me, he was a member of the investigation team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you to look at your screen, page 35 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Line 8, comes that, as far as spelling is concerned, closest to what you had in mind or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it could be different, would you please spell out as far as you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Alexei is okay. R-u-m-y-a-n-t-s-e-v.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know his rank?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he was major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time he was conducting the investigation, was that his Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 18156 to 18165. rank?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you as far as I remember major. But captain could be as well, but it seems to be major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he party to a particular investigation, perhaps a UN investigation into the incident? Did he inform you of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, UNMO team conducted investigation of their own. It was not a part of UNPROFOR investigation team. It was separate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you, sir, as to why -- at least did he inform you of the reasons for his conclusion you testified that he had told you, that it could not have been a mortar --

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- That exploded in the market? Did he tell you why he based this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I should say that during our informal conversation, he told us that a report was sent to New York. So this conversation was -- took place after the investigation was completed, officially completed, and the report was sent out. So as far as I remember, he mentioned that trajectory of the shell -- so the place of the explosion couldn't be at the place -- at that place -- just a moment. I will rephrase it. So the mortar shell trajectory can be so calculated or figured out. And if it's shelled from the Serbian side. And these normal artillery calculations shows that the shell couldn't hit the place of the explosion. Is it understood, what I try to tell?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat what you said. Did he tell you that the mortar could not have come from the Serb side or --

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Judging from the possible trajectory is the first reason. The second reason, that the direction of fragments left after the explosion on asphalt showed it couldn't be from the Serbian side. And the second -- the might -- a number of fragments of the explosion was so huge that any -- and a number of victims was very big. It couldn't be done by mortar shell, by mortar round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is he told you that it could not have been a mortar shell or that the shell could not have originated from the Serb side? Which of it?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Both. It can be -- if it were a shell -- a mortar shell, it couldn't come from Serbian side. But the character of the explosion shows that the explosion was bigger than any mortar -- any mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what it would have been?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. So his supposition was that a special explosion device was brought into the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that a UN investigation was conducted into this explosion?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was approximately one month later after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a team of experts, including artillery and mortar experts, comprised this -- the team of investigators who investigated into the explosion?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I haven't read official papers. I only say you what I heard from the person who participated in that. And I have no reasons not to believe him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, may I ask for a clarification. When you were told this by this major or captain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was left open. It might have been a major. Did he tell you about his personal impression or did he tell you about what the findings of the investigation had been as reported to the UN? Because you said something about UN report to be sent to New York.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So was he telling you what the findings had been as reported, or did he tell you that apart from what was in the report, that his personal opinion was and then et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I didn't put questions -- my questions to him in such a way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- You do now, because I never thought that I'll testify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then perhaps would you tell us what your impression was, whether he relayed to you the content of the -- of the -- the results of the investigation as reported or something different from that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was a combination, mixed up of the results which were reported and his personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would these -- this personal opinion, then, be in conformity with what was reported, or was it additionally and not in conformity with the official report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- I should say it was his comments, his personal comments which were not included. I think so. Especially when I asked him "What do you think about what was the reason of the explosion?" And he told me that some special device was brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But on the two specific issues you just mentioned, that is, the first one that the shell -- if it would have been a mortar shell, that it could never have originated from the Serbian -- from any Serbian position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second, that the -- the injuries -- or the results on the marketplace could never have caused by a mortar shell. These specific two parts, did you have the impression that he then reflected what was reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this was not a personal opinion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Apart from -- but you got the impression that when he told you these two conclusions, that that were the official conclusion that is had been reported to New York.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a feeling that it was part of the official report because being a military and judging from the investigation, it would be two main questions that any expert would ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And he did not show any disagreement in this respect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- With what you got the impression was the official finding of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was -- it went along. So it was no disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this person, are you aware that he's an expert or was a UN expert in any form, either an artillery or mortar expert?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. It seems to be no. He was not an artillery by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to my question, sir: Are you aware that a team of experts -- UN experts conducted an investigation into this explosion? Are you aware of that? I'm not --

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Asking you whether you read the documents, but are you aware?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware. I know because I've been to engineer sections and I had a number of conversations related to that. And frankly speaking, it was -- the explosion had so much impact that on many developments inside and outside Sarajevo that attention of all UN personnel was drawn to the explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that there was a person by the name of Rumyantsev. I'll spell that for you. R-u-m-y-a-n-t-s-e-v, the initial being N., lieutenant colonel, a Russian, who was included in the team?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, not lieutenant colonel. Probably he is now lieutenant colonel. I do not know. But I told you major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do agree this is one and the same person. The person who spoke to you in fact was also on the team of experts who investigated into the explosion.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least he told me so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that after the investigation, a report was compiled on the findings and forwarded to New York?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you also aware that it's reported in that report compiled by the experts which also included the person you referred to, Lieutenant Colonel, pardon my pronunciation, Rumyantsev, that the explosion was caused by a conventional factory-produced 120-millimetre mortar bomb. The mortar bomb detonated upon impact with the ground. Did you know, sir, that there was a report to such effect?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, didn't I hear the witness testify that he has not seen any report or document in this respect? So to ask him -- he testified about what he heard. Of course, if you want to use your time on that. But isn't it clear that the witness did testify --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that a number of teams were working -- expert teams were working -- investigating the explosion, separate teams. As far as I remember, it was UNPROFOR team and UNMO team. I speak to you about my conversation with UNMO officer, and probably you're now speaking about another expert report. I do not know, but I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Or did you discuss the content of such documents, apart from the conversation you just mentioned, with a person you identified as Rumyantsev? Did you speak with anyone else about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that this person whom you referred to, Lieutenant Colonel Rumyantsev, has signed and compiled a report together with other experts who investigated into the explosion, a report which in fact concludes that it was a mortar shell and in fact also which indicates the trajectory and the direction from which the shell came.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know about his signature to the report, but the only thing I told, that during our informal conversation he told me what I already pronounced. That is all. I can nothing add to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that your testimony that this very person who has in fact signed an official document and reported on his findings, which is quite contrary to what you stated here, is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before -- what is unacceptable, Ms. Mahindaratne? Is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: His testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: His --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The testimony of the witness, Mr. President. May I rephrase? May I rephrase, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that your testimony that this very person who signed a report which indicates findings that are quite contrary to what you just stated here, that is, that this person told you that it could not have been a mortar bomb and that it could not have originated from Serbian territory, is unacceptable in that your testimony -- that this same person who told you this fact is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object, because the word "unacceptable" has a moral meaning, and I think to repeat it twice would be even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne puts it to you that she has difficulties in believing that this person of which Ms. Mahindaratne says that he signed the report with contrary conclusions would have told you as the results of the investigation a totally different finding and asks you to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if he signed anything, first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I have not seen any report, first. Second, I see no reason why he should tell me the things contrary to what -- to the report that his team was -- worked at. So again, I -- I told you only about our conversation, and I cannot prove or disprove what he told me. But I have -- I see no reason what -- why he should tell me untruth facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or - and that might be part of the question as well - whether you would tell any untrue facts. I take it that this testimony includes that you're answering -- that you have answered those questions on this conversation to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The subject has been sufficiently dealt with, Ms. Mahindaratne. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to document P2261 and the English translation P2261A, which is a report which has already been tendered by the Prosecution in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's even already admitted into evidence, if I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified about sniper alley, and you stated that this was a very dangerous area. Could you clarify as to why you used the word "dangerous."

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rather open area just at the bottom of the valley, and it was exposed to any gunfire from hills. From one side -- so and those hills were places of both Muslim soldiers and Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that we can be as precise as possible, I do not recall that the witness had specifically mentioned what we know as being the street as called sniper alley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, he used the German term for that. He said "sniper strasse."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you are -- from the north. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take note. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it your position then that being exposed to the hills, your words, there was sniping from the hills towards the street?

utterances.speaker: SERGEY  MOROZ [Resumed]
